facts.label: Conflicts and source-quality flags
facts.text: 1. Term loan principal after the Third Amendment. 10-K FY2025 page:152 states "for a total principal amount of $767.8 million". 10-Q Q1 2026 page:18 and 10-Q Q2 2026 page:18 state "for a total principal amount of $772 million". The 10-Q Q2 2026 page:18 also states "As of June 30, 2026, the principal of the term note outstanding was $764.0 million." Effect: the committed term loan size is stated two ways; the outstanding principal is the figure to use for leverage, with the conflict kept visible. Not reconciled here. 2. Seemann consideration. 10-K FY2025 page:152 gives "$210.0 million in cash" plus shares valued at "$10.0 million", as agreed on December 31, 2025. 10-Q Q2 2026 page:15 gives "approximately (i) $215.9 million in cash" and shares "with an aggregate value equal to $17.0 million", and "Total consideration transferred was $232.9 million." The cash flow statement line is net of cash acquired (10-Q Q2 2026 page:4 "Acquisitions of businesses, net of cash acquired"). Effect: the transaction-summary consumer must state which basis it uses. Not reconciled here. 3. Purchase accounting revised. 10-Q Q2 2026 page:6 states that the Company "identified and recorded certain adjustments associated with the purchase accounting recorded for the acquisition of Seemann Composites, LLC and Materials Sciences LLC in the interim period ended March 31, 2026" and judged them immaterial. Effect: Q1 2026 balances as filed may differ from the Q2 allocation. 4. Internal control. 10-K FY2025 page:153 states "the Company’s disclosure controls and procedures were not effective at a reasonable assurance level" and 10-Q Q2 2026 page:41 states that controls "were not effective as of June 30, 2026 due to the material weaknesses". Effect: reliability risk on reported figures; it does not make any source unusable, but every consumer must carry it. 5. Backlog and remaining performance obligations are different measures. The release defines backlog as "the total value or current estimated value of existing contracts, less amounts previously invoiced" (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:2); the filing reports "$703.9 million of remaining performance obligations" (10-Q Q2 2026 page:7). The release says backlog was "$1.3 billion". Effect: the two must not be mixed; the filing figure controls where the two are compared. 6. End-market labels. The 10-K FY2025 page:95 describes "three end markets"; the 10-Q Q2 2026 page:9 table has four, adding "Maritime Defense Systems", with a prior-year value of nil while the release footnote says that revenue "was previously included within other end markets" (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:2). Effect: end-market series across FY2025 and 2026 are not like-for-like. 7. Management claims. The release statement that organic growth was "24.4%" (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1) is an attributed claim; the filing does not print an organic growth figure in the pages read. It supports narrative only.

facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: View: leverage on the company-defined Adjusted EBITDA basis stepped up through 2026 because debt principal rose from 506,767 thousand to 768,478 thousand while LTM Adjusted EBITDA rose from 145,302 thousand to 179,068 thousand, and cash generation does not yet support deleveraging without earnings growth. Net debt (notes payable principal less cash) over LTM Adjusted EBITDA was 3.25x at FY2025 and 4.00x at Q2 2026; including finance lease liabilities (which sit outside notes payable and whose costs fall below EBITDA) it was 3.81x and 4.57x. The increase has a mechanical cause that the sources show: the Third Amendment of the credit agreement raised the term loan by $265.0 million (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18) to fund the Seemann acquisition completed February 3, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:15), while LTM EBITDA carries Seemann only from that date and the filer states that pro forma information was impracticable (10-Q Q2 2026 page:16), so the ratio is probably overstated relative to a pro forma figure that the sources do not allow us to compute. Operating cash flow was negative for FY2025 and for the six months to June 30, 2026, because contract assets and receivables grew with revenue; with capital expenditure included, free cash flow was negative in every period shown except FY2024. Interest cover is moderate (3.37x LTM on Adjusted EBITDA versus cash interest paid) and falls to 2.74x after deducting LTM capex. Liquidity is adequate: cash and an undrawn $150.0 million revolver. The debt has no maturity before the term loan's April 1, 2032 date other than scheduled amortization of 5.050 US$m a year in the December 31, 2025 table and a current portion of 5.610 US$m at June 30, 2026, but the credit agreement itself is not supplied, the term loan size is stated two ways, and the filer reports material weaknesses in internal control. These points limit confidence in the base but do not stop the analysis. The figures below are reported facts; every ratio is a calculation shown in the Calculations section.

facts.label: Covenant and definition review
facts.text: Maintenance covenant: none while the revolver is undrawn. 10-Q Q2 2026 page:19 states the credit agreement "requires the Company to comply with a springing financial covenant that is tested on the last day of any testing fiscal quarter if and when the outstanding principal amount of revolving credit loans exceeds an applicable threshold." The level is "less than or equal to 6.50 to 1.00" for the Consolidated First Lien Net Leverage Ratio. The filer says the covenant "was not required" at June 30, 2026 and that it was in compliance. The applicable threshold, the definition of the ratio, its EBITDA add-backs and cash-netting limits are not supplied, so headroom against the covenant is Not calculable. For orientation only, net debt over Adjusted EBITDA is 4.00x and over unadjusted EBITDA 4.54x; neither uses the covenant definition, and net debt here includes the term note and other notes.

facts.label: Covenant and definition review
facts.text: Definitions that differ from the computed metric: the company's Adjusted EBITDA adds back transaction related expenses, integration and restructuring costs, lender and administrative agent fees, share-based compensation and other non-recurring costs (10-Q Q2 2026 page:35). Depreciation and amortization in the reconciliation differs from the income statement line because it includes depreciation allocated to cost of goods sold (10-K FY2025 page:102 states $11.3 million for FY2025). The add-backs recur alongside the acquisition programme (transaction costs in every period shown) and lender fees recur with each credit agreement amendment, so the adjusted measure is a weaker guide to cash earnings than the reported EBITDA beside it. EBITDA also excludes finance lease interest and right-of-use amortization (10-Q Q2 2026 page:19), which is why the lease-inclusive ratio rows are shown.

facts.label: Cash flow quality
facts.text: Operating cash flow was $26,645 thousand in FY2024, $(22,119) thousand in FY2025 and $(2,975) thousand for the six months to June 30, 2026, against $(30,955) thousand for the same months of 2025. The filings tie the weakness to working capital: for the six months to June 30, 2026 "an increase in contract assets of $24.9 million" and "an increase in accounts receivable of $25.5 million" (10-Q Q2 2026 pages 38-39 and page:4). Contract assets, which are unbilled revenue, rose from $156,298 thousand at December 31, 2025 to $187,120 thousand at June 30, 2026, an increase of $30,822 thousand on the balance sheet. Cash paid for interest and taxes continued, so the funding of the first half 2026 (capex $21,865 thousand and acquisitions $210,000 thousand) came from financing: net cash provided by financing activities was $252,235 thousand against operating cash used of $2,975 thousand (10-Q Q2 2026 page:4). Quarterly cash flow is not printed; the second quarter of 2026 is derivable only as six months less the first quarter (operating cash flow of $209 thousand in Q1 2026 per 10-Q Q1 2026 page:4 would imply $(3,184) thousand for Q2 2026), and that derived figure is not used elsewhere.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: View: Karman is a supplier of mission-critical structures, interstage systems and propulsion components to prime contractors on US missile, hypersonic, space-launch and, since February 2026, maritime defense programs. The credit story is demand-led growth that management is funding largely with acquisitions and term debt. Revenue visibility is high on paper, because the company says it often holds sole or single source positions on long-lived programs (10-K FY2025 page:17) and reports a large backlog (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1). Three features limit how far that visibility supports debt service. First, concentration: the three largest customers were about half of FY2025 revenue (10-K FY2025 page:25), so a single prime's resourcing or funding decision moves the group. Second, the backlog definition was widened in 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:33) and remaining performance obligations are a narrower measure (10-Q Q2 2026 page:7), so backlog growth cannot be read as the same kind of coverage as in the annual report. Third, the growth rate depends on acquired businesses: Seemann contributed revenue from its acquisition on February 3, 2026 (amounts in the transaction section), and the filer states that pro forma information is impracticable to obtain (10-Q Q2 2026 page:16). The ownership position is not documented in the pack: the 10-K incorporates ownership, related-party and director information by reference to a proxy statement that is not supplied (10-K FY2025 page:156), the run context names no sponsor, and a July 2025 secondary offering shows existing stockholders selling (10-K FY2025 page:107). Governance evidence is mixed: documented actions show equity raised at IPO, no dividends and no debt-funded distributions in the periods covered, but also five credit agreement amendments in the sixteen months from April 1, 2025 to August 3, 2026, and disclosed material weaknesses in internal control (10-K FY2025 page:153; 10-Q Q2 2026 page:41). Leverage and liquidity consequences are those in the financials handoff; this module adds the business mechanics behind them.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: Financing history. Before April 2025 the company borrowed under a TCW financing agreement, which was extinguished when the company entered the Citibank credit agreement on April 1, 2025 with a new $300.0 million term loan and a $50.0 million revolver, maturing April 1, 2032 and April 1, 2030 respectively (10-K FY2025 page:140). That agreement has been amended five times to the cutoff. The First Amendment on May 27, 2025 added $75.0 million of term loan to fund the ISP acquisition; the Second Amendment on October 24, 2025 added $130.0 million to fund Five Axis and repay revolver borrowings (10-K FY2025 page:140). The Third Amendment on February 2, 2026 refinanced $502.8 million of existing term loans to a margin 75 basis points lower and added $265.0 million (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). The Fourth Amendment on March 9, 2026 raised revolver commitments by $100.0 million to $150.0 million and removed the cap on incremental revolving commitments (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). The Fifth Amendment on August 3, 2026 lowered the term loan margin to SOFR plus 2.25% and revolver pricing by 50 basis points (10-Q Q2 2026 page:19). All five are completed. Each of the three term loan increases coincided with an acquisition (ISP, Five Axis, Seemann), and MTI was funded by a $30.0 million revolver draw (10-K FY2025 page:141). That is the transmission mechanism: acquisition funding is arranged by amending the existing facility, whose springing covenant is written on a first lien ratio, and not by a new issue to bond investors, so no new notes were issued in the period. No bond, note issue or ratings event appears in the sources, and the run context lists no ratings.

facts.label: Credit translations
facts.text: 1. Customer concentration. Evidence: the three largest customers were "approximately 51.5% of revenue" (10-K FY2025 page:25), yet no single program was more than 12% on average (10-K FY2025 page:10). Mechanic: demand and cash collection run through a few primes, so one customer's resourcing or payment timing changes revenue and contract assets together, which the working-capital growth in CP-1 already shows. Implication: cash conversion and revenue durability carry customer-specific risk that diversification by program does not remove; monitor customer mix and receivable and contract asset ageing. The conflict log below, on end-market shares, counters the use of the end-market split as a diversification argument. 2. Acquisition-led growth. Evidence: four closings and one pending agreement in sixteen months, each paired with a term loan increase (10-K FY2025 page:140; 10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). Mechanic: leverage is set by the pace of deals as well as earnings; LTM earnings include acquired businesses only from their closing dates, so reported leverage lags pro forma leverage while integration and transaction costs recur as add-backs. Implication: leverage tolerance depends on whether acquired earnings arrive on plan and whether further deals are debt-funded; the Walker funding is the next test. The Seemann consideration conflict counters any precise transaction-value statement. 3. Backlog visibility. Evidence: backlog is now described as including purchase orders, long term agreements and authorizations to proceed, and "Backlog was previously referred to as funded backlog" (10-Q Q2 2026 page:33). Mechanic: a broader backlog definition raises reported coverage without raising contracted, funded revenue, and government customers can terminate or not exercise options (10-K FY2025 page:35). Implication: use remaining performance obligations for revenue coverage and treat backlog as an attributed indicator. 4. Structure and ownership. Evidence: the company is a holding company whose sole asset is the stock of subsidiaries (10-K FY2025 page:3), and guarantors and security are not stated in the notes. Mechanic: cash and claims sit in subsidiaries, so structural position of the lenders depends on the guarantee and security package. Implication: committee readiness on recovery mechanics is limited until the credit agreement is read; no recovery conclusion is drawn here.

rows.label: Karman is a US missile, space and defense component maker with a growing backlog and a debt-funded acquisition strategy. Concentration in a few customers and an unclear owner base are the main credit questions.
The three largest customers accounted for approximately 51.5% of FY2025 revenue, although no single program exceeded 12%.
Four acquisitions closed between April 2025 and February 2026, one more is pending, and the term loan was increased three times.
Backlog is reported on a broader definition in 2026 than in the FY2025 annual report, while remaining performance obligations are a separate and smaller measure.
Existing stockholders sold shares in a July 2025 offering, the company received nothing, and no dividend is planned.
The FY2025 annual report and later filings give different consideration for the Seemann acquisition, and its end-market revenue shares disagree within the report.
Three largest customers were about 51.5% of FY2025 revenue
The company has in the past consummated acquisitions and intends to continue to pursue acquisitions
Backlog of $1.3 billion at June 30, 2026 and "exceptionally strong visibility"
Remaining performance obligations of $703.9 million at June 30, 2026, about 49.6% expected in the rest of 2026
Existing stockholders, not the company, sold shares in July 2025
No dividend planned; credit agreement restricts certain dividends and distributions
Management attributes margin gains to operating leverage
Revenue from Seemann is reported separately from the Maritime end market, and the two amounts differ
Ownership percentages, sponsor and control rights
Creditor-adverse actions (priming, uptiering, drop-downs, collateral release)

Executed credit agreement and amendments: guarantors, security, baskets, incremental capacity
Walker funding, earnings, closing status and regulatory approvals
Customer names, contract type mix and end-market mapping of Seemann revenue: Not disclosed in the pages read
No ratings, market, peer or deal-term inputs in the run context
Material weaknesses and revised Seemann purchase accounting

facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: Karman is a leveraged but liquid defense and space supplier whose credit profile is weakening as acquisition debt outpaces cash generation. Its strongest support is demand-led earnings growth, with LTM Adjusted EBITDA of USD 179,068 thousand, USD 201.741 million of liquidity at June 30, 2026 and no scheduled maturity beyond about USD 5.050 million a year until the term loan matures on April 1, 2032. The weakest point is cash conversion: operating cash flow was USD (22,119) thousand in FY2025 and USD (2,975) thousand in the six months to June 30, 2026, while net leverage rose from 3.25x to 4.00x of Adjusted EBITDA. What decides the outcome is whether acquired earnings and working-capital releases reduce leverage before the pending Walker acquisition, priced at about USD 94.0 million and not yet shown to be funded, draws on liquidity or adds debt.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Net leverage has risen with each acquisition. The issuer's total debt principal was USD 768,478 thousand at June 30, 2026 against USD 506,767 thousand at December 31, 2025, almost all of it the term loan upsized to fund the Seemann acquisition, so net debt over LTM Adjusted EBITDA rose from 3.25x to 4.00x and, with finance lease liabilities that sit outside notes payable and whose costs fall below EBITDA, from 3.81x to 4.57x. Because LTM earnings include acquired businesses only from closing, the ratio probably overstates pro forma leverage, but the sources do not allow that to be measured. On unadjusted EBITDA the same net ratio is 4.54x, so the add-backs of USD 21,150 thousand (11.8% of LTM Adjusted EBITDA) matter to how leveraged the issuer looks. [Analyst Interpretation, based on CP-1 leverage and the CP-1A acquisition timeline.]

facts.label: Calculations
facts.text: 1. Change in leverage on Adjusted EBITDA, FY2025 to June 30, 2026: net 4.00x - 3.25x = 0.75x; total 4.29x - 3.49x = 0.80x; lease-inclusive net 4.57x - 3.81x = 0.76x. 2. Debt versus earnings growth: total debt principal 768,478 - 506,767 = 261,711, or 261,711 / 506,767 = 51.6%; LTM Adjusted EBITDA 179,068 against FY2025 145,302 gives (179,068 - 145,302) / 145,302 = 23.2%. Debt grew faster than earnings on these bases, consistent with leverage rising. 3. Rate sensitivity: term note principal 763,962 x 1% = 7,640 per year of additional interest for a one percent rise in the floating rate (an analyst calculation, not a company figure); against LTM cash interest paid of 53,144 this is 7,640 / 53,144 = 14.4%. 4. Interest cover after the August 2026 repricing is not calculated: the company's expected annual saving is described as approximately USD 4 million and a post-amendment cash interest run rate is Not supplied. 5. Liquidity use if Walker were funded entirely from cash and revolver: 94.0 / 201.741 = 46.6%, as in the financials handoff; the funding source is Not supplied.

2. Debt versus earnings growth: total debt principal 768,478 - 506,767 = 261,711, or 261,711 / 506,767 = 51.6%; LTM Adjusted EBITDA 179,068 against FY2025 145,302 gives (179,068 - 145,302) / 145,302 = 23.2%. Debt grew faster than earnings on these bases, consistent with leverage rising.

3. Rate sensitivity: term note principal 763,962 x 1% = 7,640 per year of additional interest for a one percent rise in the floating rate (an analyst calculation, not a company figure); against LTM cash interest paid of 53,144 this is 7,640 / 53,144 = 14.4%.

5. Liquidity use if Walker were funded entirely from cash and revolver: 94.0 / 201.741 = 46.6%, as in the financials handoff; the funding source is Not supplied.

rows.label: Karman is a leveraged but liquid defense supplier whose credit profile is weakening as acquisition debt outpaces cash generation. Strong demand and USD 201.741 million of liquidity support it; cash conversion and customer concentration are the weak points.
Net debt to LTM Adjusted EBITDA rose from 3.25x at FY2025 to 4.00x at June 30, 2026, or 4.57x including finance leases.
Operating cash flow was negative in FY2025 and in the first six months of 2026, so free cash flow was negative after capex.
Liquidity of USD 201.741 million and scheduled amortization of about USD 5.050 million a year, with the bulk due on April 1, 2032, limit near-term refinancing pressure.
The three largest customers were approximately 51.5% of FY2025 revenue and material weaknesses in internal control remain.

Fundamental credit view: leveraged and rising, adequately liquid, with weak cash conversion and customer concentration; business risk supported by long-lived defense and space programs. Confidence is below High because the readiness view for this module is READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS, the credit agreement and ownership are not supplied and filed figures conflict.

Thesis: growth in defense and space demand supports earnings, but acquisition-funded leverage and negative free cash flow leave the issuer dependent on continued earnings growth and open credit markets to delever.
Executed credit agreement and amendments not supplied: covenant threshold and definition, guarantors, security, incremental capacity
Ownership, sponsor and control rights: Not supplied
Walker funding, earnings and closing status; no evidence after August 6, 2026
LTM earnings not pro forma for acquisitions

facts.label: Evidence trace view
facts.text: The analysis is traceable enough for a restricted committee read, and the most important provenance gap is the missing credit agreement. Of the claims traced, the figures in the financials handoff are Directly Sourced or Calculated, and every calculated cell reproduced from its inputs. The business handoff is mostly Directly Sourced, with a small set of Analyst Interpretations that it tags as such. One claim failed the trace: the business and credit views treat the backlog definition as having widened between the annual report and the 2026 quarterly reports, when the annual report's own key-measure note already carries the 2026 wording and states that no historical amount changed (10-K FY2025 page:99), while a risk-factor paragraph in the same annual report still uses the narrower wording (10-K FY2025 page:35). That is an unsupported directional claim, not a numeric error, and its consequence is that backlog cannot be used as evidence of a definitional change; it remains a management-reported measure that exceeds remaining performance obligations by a growing margin. The other defects are smaller. The strongest contrary evidence to the overall credit view is the liquidity position, and what would make it win is a post-amendment cash interest run rate and a funded Walker closing, both outside the sources. Committee status is Restricted: the financial and business conclusions may be used with the corrections below, and legal, covenant and recovery conclusions may not, because the credit agreement is absent.

Issuer: Karman Holdings Inc. (ticker KRMN, Delaware corporation, formerly TCFIII Spaceco Holdings LLC). As-of date: 2026-11-05. Cutoff: 2026-11-05. Pathway: credit_snapshot. Reporting currency: USD, in thousands in the filed statements. Current period q2-2026 (quarter and six months ended June 30, 2026); prior period fy-2025 (year ended December 31, 2025).

Question for this module: can the seven supplied filings and releases support the requested downstream work (financial and credit metrics, business and transaction context, credit synthesis and evidence trace), and what remains blocked? This module gives a source-sufficiency view only. It gives no credit conclusion, legal interpretation or investment opinion, and it does not normalize, reconcile or calculate financial figures.

Selected consumers assessed: CP-1 (financials and credit metrics, including chart data for leverage, interest cover, liquidity and debt maturities), CP-1A (business and transaction context), CP-2 (credit synthesis) and CP-5 (evidence trace validation). Perimeter: the reporting entity is Karman Holdings Inc. and its consolidated subsidiaries (single reporting entity, single reportable segment). No separate borrower, parent, guarantor or sponsor entity is named in the run context (borrower, parent, guarantors and sponsor are blank there; blank is not treated as none). The credit agreement names the Company as party with Citibank, N.A. as Administrative Agent and Collateral Agent.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

### Readiness view

Overall view: READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS for all four selected consumers. The effective source set is a complete filed chain for the requested pathway: one audited annual report, three unaudited quarterly reports covering the quarters ended September 30, 2025, March 31, 2026 and June 30, 2026, and three earnings releases. Each owner can perform its method on located evidence. No consumer is CONDITIONAL or BLOCKED, because no required source is missing that would stop an owner's workflow and no identity boundary is unresolved. Strongest contrary evidence: the financing documents that govern the debt are absent and the filings disagree on one debt figure (see Conflicts below), the filer reports unremediated material weaknesses, and the evidence stops at the August 2026 release although the as-of date is 2026-11-05. Those points bound the downstream work; they do not prevent it. Source sufficiency is distinct from completion of downstream analysis: no metric has been computed or accepted here. The next evidence action is to obtain the executed credit agreement with all amendments (or at minimum the Third and Fifth Amendments) and any filing made after 2026-08-06 and on or before 2026-11-05.

### Conflicts and source-quality flags

1. Term loan principal after the Third Amendment. 10-K FY2025 page:152 states "for a total principal amount of $767.8 million". 10-Q Q1 2026 page:18 and 10-Q Q2 2026 page:18 state "for a total principal amount of $772 million". The 10-Q Q2 2026 page:18 also states "As of June 30, 2026, the principal of the term note outstanding was $764.0 million." Effect: the committed term loan size is stated two ways; the outstanding principal is the figure to use for leverage, with the conflict kept visible. Not reconciled here.

2. Seemann consideration. 10-K FY2025 page:152 gives "$210.0 million in cash" plus shares valued at "$10.0 million", as agreed on December 31, 2025. 10-Q Q2 2026 page:15 gives "approximately (i) $215.9 million in cash" and shares "with an aggregate value equal to $17.0 million", and "Total consideration transferred was $232.9 million." The cash flow statement line is net of cash acquired (10-Q Q2 2026 page:4 "Acquisitions of businesses, net of cash acquired"). Effect: the transaction-summary consumer must state which basis it uses. Not reconciled here.

3. Purchase accounting revised. 10-Q Q2 2026 page:6 states that the Company "identified and recorded certain adjustments associated with the purchase accounting recorded for the acquisition of Seemann Composites, LLC and Materials Sciences LLC in the interim period ended March 31, 2026" and judged them immaterial. Effect: Q1 2026 balances as filed may differ from the Q2 allocation.

4. Internal control. 10-K FY2025 page:153 states "the Company’s disclosure controls and procedures were not effective at a reasonable assurance level" and 10-Q Q2 2026 page:41 states that controls "were not effective as of June 30, 2026 due to the material weaknesses". Effect: reliability risk on reported figures; it does not make any source unusable, but every consumer must carry it.

5. Backlog and remaining performance obligations are different measures. The release defines backlog as "the total value or current estimated value of existing contracts, less amounts previously invoiced" (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:2); the filing reports "$703.9 million of remaining performance obligations" (10-Q Q2 2026 page:7). The release says backlog was "$1.3 billion". Effect: the two must not be mixed; the filing figure controls where the two are compared.

6. End-market labels. The 10-K FY2025 page:95 describes "three end markets"; the 10-Q Q2 2026 page:9 table has four, adding "Maritime Defense Systems", with a prior-year value of nil while the release footnote says that revenue "was previously included within other end markets" (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:2). Effect: end-market series across FY2025 and 2026 are not like-for-like.

7. Management claims. The release statement that organic growth was "24.4%" (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1) is an attributed claim; the filing does not print an organic growth figure in the pages read. It supports narrative only.
### Model-input source sufficiency

Assertion: SOURCE_SUFFICIENCY_ONLY; CP_MODEL_INPUT_CONTRACT_NOT_EVALUATED. For an HTML model objective the supplied sources contain: discrete quarters from the 10-Qs and Q4 2025 from the March release; fiscal-year statements from the 10-K; quarter and year-to-date distinctions in the same statements; one segment with four end-market revenue lines; the add-back table; backlog and outlook in the releases; facility-level debt in the notes; and cash-paid interest and tax in supplemental disclosures. Not asserted: normalized quarters, reconciliation of figures across sources, or acceptance of any downstream input.
## Calculations

No financial figure was calculated, normalized or reconciled in this module, by design. The only arithmetic is a coverage count of located text pages from the pinned files: 160 + 51 + 41 + 46 + 10 + 9 + 9 = 326 pages. This count is a size indicator only and is not offered as evidence of readiness.

### Financial base view

View: leverage on the company-defined Adjusted EBITDA basis stepped up through 2026 because debt principal rose from 506,767 thousand to 768,478 thousand while LTM Adjusted EBITDA rose from 145,302 thousand to 179,068 thousand, and cash generation does not yet support deleveraging without earnings growth. Net debt (notes payable principal less cash) over LTM Adjusted EBITDA was 3.25x at FY2025 and 4.00x at Q2 2026; including finance lease liabilities (which sit outside notes payable and whose costs fall below EBITDA) it was 3.81x and 4.57x. The increase has a mechanical cause that the sources show: the Third Amendment of the credit agreement raised the term loan by $265.0 million (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18) to fund the Seemann acquisition completed February 3, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:15), while LTM EBITDA carries Seemann only from that date and the filer states that pro forma information was impracticable (10-Q Q2 2026 page:16), so the ratio is probably overstated relative to a pro forma figure that the sources do not allow us to compute. Operating cash flow was negative for FY2025 and for the six months to June 30, 2026, because contract assets and receivables grew with revenue; with capital expenditure included, free cash flow was negative in every period shown except FY2024. Interest cover is moderate (3.37x LTM on Adjusted EBITDA versus cash interest paid) and falls to 2.74x after deducting LTM capex. Liquidity is adequate: cash and an undrawn $150.0 million revolver. The debt has no maturity before the term loan's April 1, 2032 date other than scheduled amortization of 5.050 US$m a year in the December 31, 2025 table and a current portion of 5.610 US$m at June 30, 2026, but the credit agreement itself is not supplied, the term loan size is stated two ways, and the filer reports material weaknesses in internal control. These points limit confidence in the base but do not stop the analysis. The figures below are reported facts; every ratio is a calculation shown in the Calculations section.

### Covenant and definition review

Maintenance covenant: none while the revolver is undrawn. 10-Q Q2 2026 page:19 states the credit agreement "requires the Company to comply with a springing financial covenant that is tested on the last day of any testing fiscal quarter if and when the outstanding principal amount of revolving credit loans exceeds an applicable threshold." The level is "less than or equal to 6.50 to 1.00" for the Consolidated First Lien Net Leverage Ratio. The filer says the covenant "was not required" at June 30, 2026 and that it was in compliance. The applicable threshold, the definition of the ratio, its EBITDA add-backs and cash-netting limits are not supplied, so headroom against the covenant is Not calculable. For orientation only, net debt over Adjusted EBITDA is 4.00x and over unadjusted EBITDA 4.54x; neither uses the covenant definition, and net debt here includes the term note and other notes.

Definitions that differ from the computed metric: the company's Adjusted EBITDA adds back transaction related expenses, integration and restructuring costs, lender and administrative agent fees, share-based compensation and other non-recurring costs (10-Q Q2 2026 page:35). Depreciation and amortization in the reconciliation differs from the income statement line because it includes depreciation allocated to cost of goods sold (10-K FY2025 page:102 states $11.3 million for FY2025). The add-backs recur alongside the acquisition programme (transaction costs in every period shown) and lender fees recur with each credit agreement amendment, so the adjusted measure is a weaker guide to cash earnings than the reported EBITDA beside it. EBITDA also excludes finance lease interest and right-of-use amortization (10-Q Q2 2026 page:19), which is why the lease-inclusive ratio rows are shown.
### Cash flow quality

Operating cash flow was $26,645 thousand in FY2024, $(22,119) thousand in FY2025 and $(2,975) thousand for the six months to June 30, 2026, against $(30,955) thousand for the same months of 2025. The filings tie the weakness to working capital: for the six months to June 30, 2026 "an increase in contract assets of $24.9 million" and "an increase in accounts receivable of $25.5 million" (10-Q Q2 2026 pages 38-39 and page:4). Contract assets, which are unbilled revenue, rose from $156,298 thousand at December 31, 2025 to $187,120 thousand at June 30, 2026, an increase of $30,822 thousand on the balance sheet. Cash paid for interest and taxes continued, so the funding of the first half 2026 (capex $21,865 thousand and acquisitions $210,000 thousand) came from financing: net cash provided by financing activities was $252,235 thousand against operating cash used of $2,975 thousand (10-Q Q2 2026 page:4). Quarterly cash flow is not printed; the second quarter of 2026 is derivable only as six months less the first quarter (operating cash flow of $209 thousand in Q1 2026 per 10-Q Q1 2026 page:4 would imply $(3,184) thousand for Q2 2026), and that derived figure is not used elsewhere.
### Subsequent events and the latest quarter
- Third Amendment, February 2, 2026: term loans refinanced at SOFR plus 2.75% (75 basis points lower) and increased by $265.0 million; revolver pricing 75 basis points lower (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18).
- Seemann Composites and Materials Sciences acquired February 3, 2026 for total consideration of $232.9 million (10-Q Q2 2026 page:15); funded with incremental term borrowing (same page).

- Fourth Amendment, March 9, 2026: revolver commitments raised to $150.0 million from $50.0 million; debt issuance costs of $4.9 million for the amendments (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18; EX-99.1 May 2026 page:1).

- Walker Precision Engineering agreement, July 20, 2026: aggregate consideration of approximately $94.0 million, expected to close in the third quarter of 2026 subject to regulatory approvals (10-Q Q2 2026 page:29). The funding source is not stated in the sources. Closing status at the cutoff is Not supplied.

- Fifth Amendment, August 3, 2026: term loan margin reduced to SOFR plus 2.25% and revolver pricing 50 basis points lower (10-Q Q2 2026 page:19). The release expects annual interest expense lower by "approximately $4 million" (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1).

- Outlook raised on August 6, 2026 to $730 million to $745 million of revenue and $215.0 million to $222.5 million of Adjusted EBITDA for FY2026, excluding future acquisitions (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:2). This is a management projection, not evidence of results.

- Purchase accounting for Seemann was revised in Q2 2026; the filer judged the errors immaterial (10-Q Q2 2026 page:6). Disclosure controls were reported as not effective at June 30, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:41).
### Consistency with the upstream handoff

The source-readiness handoff listed the term loan size conflict and the Seemann consideration conflict. Re-checked against the filings, both stand: the 10-K FY2025 page:152 gives a total term loan principal of $767.8 million after the Third Amendment, while 10-Q Q1 2026 page:18 and 10-Q Q2 2026 page:18 give "$772 million". This answer uses the outstanding principal at each balance sheet date (765,881 thousand at March 31, 2026 on 10-Q Q1 2026 page:17 and 763,962 thousand at June 30, 2026 on 10-Q Q2 2026 page:18), which does not depend on the committed figure. No statement in the handoff was found to be wrong. This answer adds three items the handoff did not state: the December 31, 2024 balance sheet carried a 25,000 thousand revolver balance (included in FY2024 total debt); the only post-amendment maturity datum is the current portion of 5,610 thousand on the June 30, 2026 balance sheet; and the handoff's finding that no letters of credit or hedges were disclosed is a result of text search, which this module repeated without finding a disclosure.

### Business and transaction view

View: Karman is a supplier of mission-critical structures, interstage systems and propulsion components to prime contractors on US missile, hypersonic, space-launch and, since February 2026, maritime defense programs. The credit story is demand-led growth that management is funding largely with acquisitions and term debt. Revenue visibility is high on paper, because the company says it often holds sole or single source positions on long-lived programs (10-K FY2025 page:17) and reports a large backlog (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1). Three features limit how far that visibility supports debt service. First, concentration: the three largest customers were about half of FY2025 revenue (10-K FY2025 page:25), so a single prime's resourcing or funding decision moves the group. Second, the backlog definition was widened in 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:33) and remaining performance obligations are a narrower measure (10-Q Q2 2026 page:7), so backlog growth cannot be read as the same kind of coverage as in the annual report. Third, the growth rate depends on acquired businesses: Seemann contributed revenue from its acquisition on February 3, 2026 (amounts in the transaction section), and the filer states that pro forma information is impracticable to obtain (10-Q Q2 2026 page:16). The ownership position is not documented in the pack: the 10-K incorporates ownership, related-party and director information by reference to a proxy statement that is not supplied (10-K FY2025 page:156), the run context names no sponsor, and a July 2025 secondary offering shows existing stockholders selling (10-K FY2025 page:107). Governance evidence is mixed: documented actions show equity raised at IPO, no dividends and no debt-funded distributions in the periods covered, but also five credit agreement amendments in the sixteen months from April 1, 2025 to August 3, 2026, and disclosed material weaknesses in internal control (10-K FY2025 page:153; 10-Q Q2 2026 page:41). Leverage and liquidity consequences are those in the financials handoff; this module adds the business mechanics behind them.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues
This section is prose only. The facts are ordered by date and each states its status at the cutoff.

Financing history. Before April 2025 the company borrowed under a TCW financing agreement, which was extinguished when the company entered the Citibank credit agreement on April 1, 2025 with a new $300.0 million term loan and a $50.0 million revolver, maturing April 1, 2032 and April 1, 2030 respectively (10-K FY2025 page:140). That agreement has been amended five times to the cutoff. The First Amendment on May 27, 2025 added $75.0 million of term loan to fund the ISP acquisition; the Second Amendment on October 24, 2025 added $130.0 million to fund Five Axis and repay revolver borrowings (10-K FY2025 page:140). The Third Amendment on February 2, 2026 refinanced $502.8 million of existing term loans to a margin 75 basis points lower and added $265.0 million (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). The Fourth Amendment on March 9, 2026 raised revolver commitments by $100.0 million to $150.0 million and removed the cap on incremental revolving commitments (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). The Fifth Amendment on August 3, 2026 lowered the term loan margin to SOFR plus 2.25% and revolver pricing by 50 basis points (10-Q Q2 2026 page:19). All five are completed. Each of the three term loan increases coincided with an acquisition (ISP, Five Axis, Seemann), and MTI was funded by a $30.0 million revolver draw (10-K FY2025 page:141). That is the transmission mechanism: acquisition funding is arranged by amending the existing facility, whose springing covenant is written on a first lien ratio, and not by a new issue to bond investors, so no new notes were issued in the period. No bond, note issue or ratings event appears in the sources, and the run context lists no ratings.

Equity events. The IPO was completed on February 14, 2025: 26.5 million shares at $22.00, of which 8.4 million were sold by the company (10-K FY2025 page:116). On July 23, 2025 existing stockholders priced a secondary sale of 21,000,000 shares at $49.00, with an option for 3,150,000 more that was fully exercised, and the company "did not sell any shares or receive proceeds" (10-K FY2025 page:107). The company expects to retain earnings and has no current plans to pay dividends (10-K FY2025 page:87).

Acquisitions. MTI closed April 2, 2025 for $82.3 million in cash; ISP closed May 28, 2025 for approximately $52.9 million in cash and 147,842 shares; Five Axis closed October 28, 2025 for $90.7 million in cash and 68,625 shares (all 10-K FY2025 page:94). Seemann Composites and Materials Sciences, a maritime defense composites business, closed February 3, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:15). The Q2 2026 10-Q states cash of approximately $215.9 million, shares valued at $17.0 million and total consideration transferred of $232.9 million, funded with incremental term borrowing, while the 10-K described the signed agreement as $210.0 million in cash and $10.0 million in shares (10-K FY2025 page:152); this is logged as a conflict and not reconciled. Seemann revenue was $37.8 million for the three months and $63.0 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:16). Walker Precision Engineering, a Glasgow-based maker of components for missile seekers and guidance systems, is the subject of a definitive agreement dated July 20, 2026 for aggregate consideration of approximately $94.0 million, expected to close in the third quarter of 2026 subject to regulatory approvals (10-Q Q2 2026 page:29). Its status at the cutoff is pending as far as the sources show; funding, its earnings and any financing are Not supplied. It would be the first non-US operation described in the sources read, since the listed subsidiaries are in US states (10-Q Q2 2026 page:4); analyst interpretation: that adds cross-border integration and export-control questions the filings do not address.

Effect on leverage and liquidity. Per the financials handoff, total debt principal rose to 768,478 thousand at June 30, 2026 from 506,767 thousand at December 31, 2025 and net debt over LTM Adjusted EBITDA reached 4.00x. The debt increase is the Seemann funding. Cash and the undrawn revolver gave 201.741 US$m of liquidity, and the handoff's illustration shows the pending Walker consideration would consume 46.6% of it if funded entirely from liquidity; the sources do not say how it will be funded. The expected annual interest saving from the repricing is described by management as "approximately $4 million" (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1). Seller notes and contingent consideration: the 2024 seller note was repaid in April 2025 (10-K FY2025 page:141), and the Seemann acquisition has no contingent consideration (10-Q Q2 2026 page:15).

Evidence quality is High for primary filed facts, Medium for management statements in releases and Insufficient for ownership.
### Credit translations

1. Customer concentration. Evidence: the three largest customers were "approximately 51.5% of revenue" (10-K FY2025 page:25), yet no single program was more than 12% on average (10-K FY2025 page:10). Mechanic: demand and cash collection run through a few primes, so one customer's resourcing or payment timing changes revenue and contract assets together, which the working-capital growth in CP-1 already shows. Implication: cash conversion and revenue durability carry customer-specific risk that diversification by program does not remove; monitor customer mix and receivable and contract asset ageing. The conflict log below, on end-market shares, counters the use of the end-market split as a diversification argument.

2. Acquisition-led growth. Evidence: four closings and one pending agreement in sixteen months, each paired with a term loan increase (10-K FY2025 page:140; 10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). Mechanic: leverage is set by the pace of deals as well as earnings; LTM earnings include acquired businesses only from their closing dates, so reported leverage lags pro forma leverage while integration and transaction costs recur as add-backs. Implication: leverage tolerance depends on whether acquired earnings arrive on plan and whether further deals are debt-funded; the Walker funding is the next test. The Seemann consideration conflict counters any precise transaction-value statement.

3. Backlog visibility. Evidence: backlog is now described as including purchase orders, long term agreements and authorizations to proceed, and "Backlog was previously referred to as funded backlog" (10-Q Q2 2026 page:33). Mechanic: a broader backlog definition raises reported coverage without raising contracted, funded revenue, and government customers can terminate or not exercise options (10-K FY2025 page:35). Implication: use remaining performance obligations for revenue coverage and treat backlog as an attributed indicator.

4. Structure and ownership. Evidence: the company is a holding company whose sole asset is the stock of subsidiaries (10-K FY2025 page:3), and guarantors and security are not stated in the notes. Mechanic: cash and claims sit in subsidiaries, so structural position of the lenders depends on the guarantee and security package. Implication: committee readiness on recovery mechanics is limited until the credit agreement is read; no recovery conclusion is drawn here.
### Conflicts logged
Each conflict is logged without reconciliation.

1. Seemann consideration. 10-K FY2025 page:152: "$210.0 million in cash and (ii) shares of common stock of the Company with an aggregate value equal to $10.0 million". 10-Q Q2 2026 page:15: "approximately (i) $215.9 million in cash" and shares "with an aggregate value equal to $17.0 million", with "Total consideration transferred was $232.9 million." Effect: transaction value depends on the basis; the 10-K describes the signed agreement and the 10-Q the completed deal with adjustments.

2. Term loan principal after the Third Amendment: $767.8 million (10-K FY2025 page:152) versus $772 million (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). Effect: committed facility size is uncertain; outstanding principal is used elsewhere.

3. End-market shares within the 10-K. Item 1 states Tactical Missiles at 31.5% and Space and Launch at 36.9% of revenue (10-K FY2025 page:14), while the results table shows Space and Launch at 149,825 and Tactical Missiles at 171,688 thousand of 471,500 thousand (10-K FY2025 page:96) and page:17 states 32%, 36% and 32%. Effect: the business description labels and the table disagree on which market is largest; the table amounts are used in the Calculations.

4. IPO proceeds. 10-K FY2025 page:116 states net proceeds of "approximately $147.3 million" after deductions and payments to Phantom Unit holders, while the cash flow statement shows net proceeds of 154,836 thousand (10-K FY2025 page:115). Effect: use of proceeds and equity raised cannot be stated to one figure.

5. Backlog definition: funding "appropriated or otherwise authorized" (10-K FY2025 page:35) versus a broader contract list in the 2026 filings (10-Q Q2 2026 page:33). Effect: backlog across the FY2025 and 2026 filings is not like-for-like even though the company says historical amounts were not changed.

### Consistency with upstream handoffs

The readiness handoff flagged the Seemann consideration, the term loan size, the end-market taxonomy and the backlog versus remaining performance obligations; all four stand after re-checking and are carried above. This answer adds three items that handoff did not log: the within-10-K inconsistency of end-market percentages (conflict 3), the IPO net proceeds difference (conflict 4), and the fact that Seemann revenue exceeds the Maritime end-market line. The financials handoff states that liquidity and leverage figures are on an Adjusted EBITDA basis that is not pro forma; this answer's statements on acquisitions agree with it and do not change its figures. The financials handoff named acquisition dates for MTI, ISP, Five Axis and Seemann; they are confirmed on the cited pages.
## Calculations

1. End-market shares of FY2025 revenue, from the table amounts (10-K FY2025 page:96), USD thousands: Hypersonics and Strategic Missile Defense 149,987 / 471,500 = 31.8%; Space and Launch 149,825 / 471,500 = 31.8%; Tactical Missiles and Integrated Defense Systems 171,688 / 471,500 = 36.4%. Sum of amounts 149,987 + 149,825 + 171,688 = 471,500. Item 1 percentages 31.7 + 31.5 + 36.9 = 100.1.

3. Revenue growth excluding Seemann revenue, an analyst calculation that differs from the company's organic definition: Q2 2026 (182,063 - 37,800) / 115,097 - 1 = 25.3%; six months 2026 (333,273 - 63,000) / 215,221 - 1 = 25.6%. Seemann revenue is rounded from $37.8 million and $63.0 million (10-Q Q2 2026 page:16); the company's reported organic growth for Q2 2026 is 24.4% (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1) and is not recomputed here. Growth including all acquisitions is 58.2% for Q2 per the release.
4. Seemann revenue share of Q2 2026 revenue: 37,800 / 182,063 = 20.8%. Seemann revenue exceeds the Maritime line: 37,800 against 33,562 for the quarter and 63,000 against 59,970 for six months.

5. Number of amendments to the credit agreement from April 1, 2025 to the cutoff: First (May 27, 2025), Second (October 24, 2025), Third (February 2, 2026), Fourth (March 9, 2026), Fifth (August 3, 2026) = 5, over the period April 1, 2025 to August 3, 2026 (about sixteen months). Acquisitions closed between April 2, 2025 and February 3, 2026: MTI, ISP, Five Axis, Seemann = 4; Walker pending = 1.
6. Remaining performance obligations by period, from the stated shares of 703.9: 49.6% in remaining 2026, 23.3% in 2027, 27.1% thereafter; 49.6 + 23.3 + 27.1 = 100.0.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Karman is a leveraged but liquid defense supplier whose credit profile is weakening as acquisition debt outpaces cash generation. Strong demand and USD 201.741 million of liquidity support it; cash conversion and customer concentration are the weak points. | Medium | The credit agreement and ownership are not supplied, earnings are not pro forma for acquisitions, and several filed figures conflict. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Net debt to LTM Adjusted EBITDA rose from 3.25x at FY2025 to 4.00x at June 30, 2026, or 4.57x including finance leases. | Leverage has stepped up and sits above the level at the annual report date. | High |

| Operating cash flow was negative in FY2025 and in the first six months of 2026, so free cash flow was negative after capex. | Deleveraging needs earnings growth or a working-capital release, not internal cash. | High |

| Liquidity of USD 201.741 million and scheduled amortization of about USD 5.050 million a year, with the bulk due on April 1, 2032, limit near-term refinancing pressure. | Refinancing pressure is limited by liquidity and maturities; the pending Walker deal is the main call on cash. | Medium |

| The three largest customers were approximately 51.5% of FY2025 revenue and material weaknesses in internal control remain. | Revenue and reporting reliability carry specific risks that diversification by program does not remove. | Medium |
### Credit view

Karman is a leveraged but liquid defense and space supplier whose credit profile is weakening as acquisition debt outpaces cash generation. Its strongest support is demand-led earnings growth, with LTM Adjusted EBITDA of USD 179,068 thousand, USD 201.741 million of liquidity at June 30, 2026 and no scheduled maturity beyond about USD 5.050 million a year until the term loan matures on April 1, 2032. The weakest point is cash conversion: operating cash flow was USD (22,119) thousand in FY2025 and USD (2,975) thousand in the six months to June 30, 2026, while net leverage rose from 3.25x to 4.00x of Adjusted EBITDA. What decides the outcome is whether acquired earnings and working-capital releases reduce leverage before the pending Walker acquisition, priced at about USD 94.0 million and not yet shown to be funded, draws on liquidity or adds debt.
### Key findings

Net leverage has risen with each acquisition. The issuer's total debt principal was USD 768,478 thousand at June 30, 2026 against USD 506,767 thousand at December 31, 2025, almost all of it the term loan upsized to fund the Seemann acquisition, so net debt over LTM Adjusted EBITDA rose from 3.25x to 4.00x and, with finance lease liabilities that sit outside notes payable and whose costs fall below EBITDA, from 3.81x to 4.57x. Because LTM earnings include acquired businesses only from closing, the ratio probably overstates pro forma leverage, but the sources do not allow that to be measured. On unadjusted EBITDA the same net ratio is 4.54x, so the add-backs of USD 21,150 thousand (11.8% of LTM Adjusted EBITDA) matter to how leveraged the issuer looks. [Analyst Interpretation, based on CP-1 leverage and the CP-1A acquisition timeline.]

The issuer does not yet generate free cash. Operating cash flow was USD (22,119) thousand in FY2025 and USD (2,975) thousand in the six months to June 30, 2026, and operating cash flow less capex was USD (27,671) thousand on an LTM basis, as contract assets rose from USD 156,298 thousand to USD 187,120 thousand. Interest, capex and acquisitions were therefore paid from new debt and, in 2025, the IPO. The mechanism is revenue recognized over time ahead of billing, so growth consumes cash until contracts bill and collect. [Documentary Fact for the figures; Analyst Interpretation for the mechanism.]

Liquidity and maturities are the main support. Cash of USD 51.741 million plus an undrawn revolver of USD 150.0 million gave USD 201.741 million at June 30, 2026, scheduled amortization is about USD 5.050 million a year with USD 481.517 million shown as due thereafter in the December 31, 2025 schedule, the term loan matures on April 1, 2032 and the revolver on April 1, 2030. The one financial covenant is springing at 6.50x on a first lien net leverage basis and applies only when the revolver is drawn beyond a threshold the sources do not state, so lenders have no maintenance test while it is undrawn. [Documentary Fact.]

Customer and counterparty concentration is the main business risk. The three largest customers were approximately 51.5% of FY2025 revenue and no single program exceeded 12%, so revenue depends on a few primes even though the program base is broad. The filer's claim of sole or single source positions is management language and is not independently verified. [Documentary Fact for the percentages; Management Language for the positions.]

Reported information is less reliable than a clean filer's. Material weaknesses in internal control were reported as not remediated at June 30, 2026, Seemann purchase accounting was revised in the second quarter and judged immaterial, and the filings conflict on the Seemann consideration (cash of USD 210.0 million in the annual report against approximately USD 215.9 million cash and USD 232.9 million total consideration later), the term loan size (USD 767.8 million against USD 772 million) and end-market revenue shares. Each is logged and not reconciled. [Documentary Fact.]
### Strengths and weaknesses
Strengths.

Demand and positioning. The issuer supplies payload protection, interstage and propulsion systems to US missile, hypersonic, launch and maritime programs, and management says it often holds sole or single source positions. The mechanism is that qualified suppliers are rarely requalified, which supports revenue durability, but the claim is management's. [Management Language, CP-1A company and operating model rows.]

Earnings scale and margin. LTM revenue was USD 589,552 thousand and LTM Adjusted EBITDA USD 179,068 thousand, a margin of 30.4%, with gross margin of 41.7% LTM against 38.3% in FY2024. Higher earnings are what reduces leverage if debt stays flat. [Documentary Fact, CP-1.]

Liquidity and maturity profile. Liquidity of USD 201.741 million at June 30, 2026, an undrawn revolver of USD 150.0 million, and a current portion of notes of USD 5.610 million with the term loan due April 1, 2032 mean no refinancing event is near. [Documentary Fact, CP-1.]
Program breadth. No single program was more than 12% of revenue, which limits single-program loss risk even with customer concentration. [Documentary Fact, CP-1A.]

Interest burden covered. LTM Adjusted EBITDA covered cash interest paid 3.37x, 3.24x in FY2025, and the August 3, 2026 repricing lowers future cash interest. [Documentary Fact for the ratios; Analyst Interpretation for the direction of future interest.]
Weaknesses.

Leverage drift. Net debt over Adjusted EBITDA rose from 3.25x to 4.00x and total debt over Adjusted EBITDA from 3.49x to 4.29x, because debt grew faster than LTM earnings. The mechanism is debt-funded acquisitions whose earnings enter LTM only from closing. [Documentary Fact for the ratios; Analyst Interpretation for the cause.]

Cash conversion. Negative operating cash flow and negative free cash flow after capex, with working capital absorbing cash as contract assets grow. Cover falls to 2.74x after deducting LTM capex, and 2.97x on unadjusted EBITDA. [Documentary Fact, CP-1.]

Concentration. The three largest customers were approximately 51.5% of FY2025 revenue and one supplier was 23.8% of accounts payable at December 31, 2025. A resourcing, funding or payment change at one prime would hit revenue and receivables together. [Documentary Fact, CP-1A.]

Acquisition dependence and add-backs. Four acquisitions closed between April 2025 and February 2026 and a fifth is pending; transaction, integration and lender fees recur as add-backs of USD 21,150 thousand LTM. The mechanism is that EBITDA quality depends on a recurring set of items. [Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation.]

Reporting reliability and thin lender protection in the sources. Unremediated material weaknesses, revised purchase accounting, five conflicts, an undisclosed owner base and no supplied credit agreement mean lender protections, guarantors and security cannot be confirmed. Missing evidence here is not an adverse conclusion; it limits confidence. [Insufficient Information for ownership and covenant terms.]

Floating-rate exposure. The term loan is priced at SOFR plus 2.25% from August 3, 2026, and no interest rate hedge was found in the sources searched, so cash interest moves with rates. [Documentary Fact; absence of hedges is Insufficient Information.]
### Credit assessment
| Assessment | Category | Confidence | Basis |

| Fundamental credit view: leveraged and rising, adequately liquid, with weak cash conversion and customer concentration; business risk supported by long-lived defense and space programs. Confidence is below High because the readiness view for this module is READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS, the credit agreement and ownership are not supplied and filed figures conflict. | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | CP-1 leverage, liquidity, cash flow and cover tables; CP-1A company, concentration, acquisition and conflict sections |

| Thesis: growth in defense and space demand supports earnings, but acquisition-funded leverage and negative free cash flow leave the issuer dependent on continued earnings growth and open credit markets to delever. | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | Same basis |
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity |

| Leverage drift from acquisitions | Term loan increases fund deals; LTM earnings include targets only from closing; Walker (about USD 94.0 million) is pending and unfunded in the sources | Leverage tolerance depends on integration and earnings catching up; a cash-funded Walker would use 46.6% of June 30 liquidity | Material |

| Weak cash conversion | Revenue recognized ahead of billing builds contract assets; capex and interest are paid in cash | Free cash flow is negative; deleveraging relies on EBITDA growth or working-capital release | Material |
| Customer concentration | Three customers were approximately 51.5% of FY2025 revenue | A single prime's budget, resourcing or payment change hits revenue and cash collection | Material |

| Reporting and controls | Material weaknesses not remediated; purchase accounting revised | Reported leverage and earnings carry reliability risk; monitoring posture should be heightened | Material |

| Lender protection unknown | Springing 6.50x covenant tests only when the revolver is drawn above an undisclosed threshold; guarantors and security not stated | No maintenance test while undrawn; structural position cannot be assessed; no recovery conclusion is drawn | Material |
| Floating-rate cost | Term loan is SOFR plus 2.25%; no hedge found | Cash interest moves with rates; a 1% change is shown in the calculations | Minor |

| Backlog interpretation | Backlog definition widened in 2026; remaining performance obligations are a narrower measure | Backlog overstates contracted, funded coverage; use remaining performance obligations for coverage | Minor |
## Calculations
All inputs are from the financials handoff (USD thousands unless stated) or the business handoff.
1. Change in leverage on Adjusted EBITDA, FY2025 to June 30, 2026: net 4.00x - 3.25x = 0.75x; total 4.29x - 3.49x = 0.80x; lease-inclusive net 4.57x - 3.81x = 0.76x.

2. Debt versus earnings growth: total debt principal 768,478 - 506,767 = 261,711, or 261,711 / 506,767 = 51.6%; LTM Adjusted EBITDA 179,068 against FY2025 145,302 gives (179,068 - 145,302) / 145,302 = 23.2%. Debt grew faster than earnings on these bases, consistent with leverage rising.

3. Rate sensitivity: term note principal 763,962 x 1% = 7,640 per year of additional interest for a one percent rise in the floating rate (an analyst calculation, not a company figure); against LTM cash interest paid of 53,144 this is 7,640 / 53,144 = 14.4%.

4. Interest cover after the August 2026 repricing is not calculated: the company's expected annual saving is described as approximately USD 4 million and a post-amendment cash interest run rate is Not supplied.
5. Liquidity use if Walker were funded entirely from cash and revolver: 94.0 / 201.741 = 46.6%, as in the financials handoff; the funding source is Not supplied.

## Calculations
Independent recomputation, from the cited inputs and not from the handoffs' own outputs, with the result of each check:

1. The financials table was recomputed by script from its own printed inputs. LTM cells (FY2025 + six months 2026 - six months 2025) for revenue, gross profit, net operating income, net interest, net income, EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA, cash interest, cash taxes, operating cash flow, capex and acquisitions: no mismatch. Gross margin and Adjusted EBITDA margin for all seven columns, add-backs, and free cash flow for all five columns: no mismatch within rounding. Total debt, net debt and all nine ratio rows for FY2024, FY2025 and LTM June 2026: no mismatch.
4. Debt schedule: 5,050 x 5 + 481,517 = 506,767, equal to the printed total.
6. Credit handoff: debt growth 261,711 / 506,767 = 51.6%; LTM earnings growth (179,068 - 145,302) / 145,302 = 23.2%; rate sensitivity 763,962 x 1% = 7,640; 7,640 / 53,144 = 14.4%. Matches.

7. New for the backlog review. Backlog per the annual report key-measure table 801,056 thousand at December 31, 2025 (10-K FY2025 page:99) and 1,322,124 thousand at June 30, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:33): growth 1,322,124 / 801,056 - 1 = 65.0%, equal to the company's 65%. Remaining performance obligations 550.6 million at December 31, 2025 (10-K FY2025 page:120) and 703.9 million at June 30, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:7): growth 703.9 / 550.6 - 1 = 27.8%. Backlog exceeds remaining performance obligations by 801.056 - 550.6 = 250.456 million at December 31, 2025 and by 1,322.124 - 703.9 = 618.224 million at June 30, 2026. Remaining performance obligations were 723.3 million at March 31, 2026 (10-Q Q1 2026 page:7), so they fell by 723.3 - 703.9 = 19.4 million in the second quarter while quarterly bookings were reported as nearly 500 million (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1). The sources do not explain the divergence; it may reflect contract types in backlog that are not remaining performance obligations, which is an interpretation and not a finding.

Corrected backlog statement for downstream use: the annual report carries two descriptions of backlog. The risk-factor paragraph says "contracts for which funding is appropriated or otherwise authorized" (10-K FY2025 page:35). The key-measure note says contract types "include but are not limited to purchase orders, long term agreements and contractual authorization to proceed" and "Backlog was previously referred to as funded backlog. No change to the historical dollar amount presented to the table above." (10-K FY2025 page:99). The 2026 quarterly report repeats the key-measure wording (10-Q Q2 2026 page:33). Whether the measure itself changed is therefore not established, and the handoffs' statement that the definition widened between the annual report and 2026 is withdrawn.
